column2: pulling a cat's tail
column3: never pull a cat's tail; stroke it gently along the back
column4: it hurts the cat and it may scratch or bite to protect itself

column2: a cat lashing or thumping its tail while you stroke it
column3: stop stroking and let the cat walk away
column4: a swishing tail means the cat is annoyed and may soon scratch or bite

column2: a cat rolls over and shows its belly
column3: admire it but do not rub the belly unless you know this cat likes it
column4: many cats show the belly to say they feel safe, not to ask for a tummy rub, and grab the hand that touches it

column2: a cat purring on your lap
column3: stroke it gently and let it leave when it wants
column4: purring usually means contentment, though cats sometimes purr when ill or in pain too

column2: a cat hisses or flattens its ears
column3: step back slowly and leave it alone
column4: hissing and flat ears are a warning that the cat feels scared or angry

column2: picking up a cat
column3: put one hand under its chest and the other under its back legs, and hold it close
column4: a cat held only under the front legs feels unsafe and its body is strained

column2: a cat brings home a dead mouse or bird
column3: do not touch it with bare hands; ask an adult to throw it away; do not scold the cat
column4: hunting is natural to cats, and dead animals can carry germs and parasites

column2: wanting to protect garden birds from your cat
column3: ask your family about a bell on a safety collar and keeping the cat in at dawn, dusk and night
column4: cats kill many wild birds, and these times are when birds feed most

column2: the cat's litter box is dirty
column3: scoop it every day with a scoop, then wash your hands; adults who are pregnant should not clean it
column4: cats refuse dirty boxes, and cat droppings can carry germs such as toxoplasma

column2: a cat scratching the sofa
column3: give it a scratching post and praise it for using it; never punish it by hitting
column4: scratching keeps a cat's claws healthy and marks its territory; it is not naughtiness

column2: giving a cat a saucer of cow's milk
column3: give the cat fresh water instead
column4: most adult cats cannot digest the sugar in milk well and get tummy upsets

column2: a cat eating grass
column3: let it, as long as the grass has no weedkiller on it
column4: cats nibble grass now and then, and sometimes bring up a hairball afterwards

column2: lilies brought into a house with a cat
column3: tell an adult; lilies should not be kept where a cat lives
column4: every part of a lily, even pollen or vase water, can badly harm a cat's kidneys

column2: a strange cat comes up to you outside
column3: hold out a finger low and let it sniff; stroke only if it rubs against you
column4: a cat you do not know may scratch, and letting it come to you is polite

column2: believing a cat always lands on its feet
column3: never drop or throw a cat, and keep windows and balconies safe
column4: cats can be badly hurt in falls, especially from balconies

column2: a cat slow-blinks at you
column3: slowly blink back
column4: a slow blink is a friendly cat signal of trust

column2: a kitten bites and scratches your hands in play
column3: play with a wand toy, not your fingers
column4: a kitten that learns hands are toys will bite harder when it grows up

column2: a cat hides under the bed after a party or fireworks
column3: leave it alone in its hiding place and keep things quiet
column4: a frightened cat calms down when it feels hidden and safe

column2: a cat that stops eating or keeps going to the litter box without passing anything
column3: tell an adult straight away
column4: these can be signs of a serious illness that needs a vet quickly

column2: a cat brushing against your legs
column3: stroke its cheek or back gently
column4: cats rub against you to leave their scent and say you belong to them

column2: meeting a dog you do not know
column3: ask the owner first, then let the dog sniff your closed hand before stroking its side
column4: a dog that does not know you may be scared and bite if surprised

column2: a dog is eating its food
column3: leave it alone until it has finished
column4: many dogs guard their food and may snap at someone who comes near the bowl

column2: a dog is sleeping
column3: do not wake it by touching it; call its name from a distance
column4: a dog woken suddenly can bite before it is properly awake

column2: hugging a dog around its neck
column3: stroke its chest or side instead of hugging
column4: most dogs feel trapped when hugged and some bite the face

column2: putting your face close to a dog's face
column3: keep your face away from the dog's face
column4: bites to children's faces often happen this way

column2: a dog showing its teeth, growling or going stiff
column3: stand still, look away, then back away slowly
column4: these are warnings that the dog may bite; running makes it chase

column2: a loose dog runs towards you
column3: stand still like a tree, arms by your sides, look at your feet, and do not run or scream
column4: running and shrieking can make a dog chase and jump

column2: a dog knocks you down
column3: curl up like a ball, cover your head and neck with your arms and stay still
column4: this protects the parts of you that matter most until help comes

column2: believing a wagging tail always means a friendly dog
column3: look at the whole dog: a stiff body and high, fast-wagging tail can mean trouble
column4: dogs wag their tails when excited or tense too, not only when happy

column2: a dog yawns, licks its lips and turns its head away
column3: give it space and stop what you are doing
column4: these are calm-down signals that the dog feels uneasy

column2: a dog with a yellow ribbon or a yellow lead
column3: do not go near the dog
column4: a yellow ribbon is used in some places to say the dog needs space

column2: a guide dog or assistance dog in a harness
column3: do not stroke, call or feed it
column4: it is working to keep its owner safe and must not be distracted

column2: a dog is tied up outside a shop
column3: do not stroke it
column4: its owner is not there to say whether it is friendly, and it cannot move away if scared

column2: a dog barking behind a fence or gate
column3: walk past calmly and do not tease it or put your fingers through
column4: dogs guard their home, and teasing teaches them to be aggressive

column2: giving a dog chocolate
column3: never give a dog chocolate
column4: chocolate contains a chemical that is poisonous to dogs

column2: sharing grapes or raisins with a dog
column3: never give dogs grapes, raisins or sultanas
column4: they can damage a dog's kidneys even in small amounts

column2: a dog finds a cooked bone
column3: do not give dogs cooked bones
column4: cooked bones splinter and can choke the dog or hurt its insides

column2: leaving a dog in a car on a warm day
column3: tell an adult right away if you see this
column4: a car heats up fast and a dog can die of heatstroke within minutes

column2: walking a dog on a hot pavement
column3: test the ground with the back of your hand for a few seconds
column4: if it is too hot for your hand, it can burn a dog's paws

column2: walking a big dog on your own
column3: walk a big or strong dog only with an adult
column4: a strong dog can pull a child over or into a road

column2: your dog does a poo in the park
column3: pick it up with a bag and put it in a bin
column4: dog poo spreads germs and worms and is unpleasant for everyone; many places fine owners who leave it

column2: letting your dog off the lead
column3: only let it off where it is allowed and when it comes back when called
column4: a dog that runs off can be hit by a car or chase farm animals

column2: training a dog to sit
column3: use a treat and praise when it sits, and keep sessions short
column4: dogs learn best with rewards and short, happy practice

column2: a dog jumps up at you
column3: turn away and fold your arms, and give attention when all four paws are on the floor
column4: this teaches the dog that jumping does not get attention

column2: throwing sticks for a dog
column3: throw a ball or a rubber toy instead
column4: sticks can splinter and stab a dog's mouth or throat

column2: a dog is shaking and hiding during fireworks or a thunderstorm
column3: stay calm nearby, let it hide, and keep doors and windows shut
column4: loud noises frighten many dogs, and a scared dog may run away

column2: a puppy chewing your shoes
column3: put shoes away and give the puppy a chew toy
column4: puppies chew to explore and soothe their teeth

column2: a dog is ill or injured and you go to help
column3: call an adult and do not touch it yourself
column4: a dog in pain may bite even its own family

column2: wanting to wash the dog
column3: only bathe it with an adult and dog shampoo, not human shampoo
column4: human shampoo can dry out and irritate a dog's skin

column2: brushing the dog
column3: brush gently in the direction the fur grows
column4: brushing removes loose hair and tangles and lets you check for ticks and lumps

column2: a dog eats something it should not, such as medicine or a sock
column3: tell an adult straight away
column4: some things can poison a dog or block its gut and need a vet

column2: picking up a rabbit by its ears
column3: never lift a rabbit by its ears; sit on the floor and let it come to you
column4: rabbits are prey animals, hate being lifted, and can hurt their backs if they kick

column2: holding a rabbit
column3: support its bottom and back legs and keep it low or sit down with it
column4: a rabbit that falls or kicks out can break its back

column2: a rabbit living alone in a small hutch
column3: rabbits need a friend of their own kind and lots of space to hop and run
column4: rabbits are social animals and get lonely and bored on their own

column2: feeding a rabbit only carrots
column3: give mostly hay, some fresh greens and a little rabbit food; carrots only as a treat
column4: carrots are sugary; hay keeps a rabbit's teeth and gut healthy

column2: a rabbit thumps its back foot
column3: check what might be scaring it and keep it calm
column4: thumping is a rabbit's warning that it senses danger

column2: a rabbit jumps and twists in the air
column3: enjoy it
column4: this jump, called a binky, means the rabbit is happy

column2: a rabbit's teeth look too long
column3: tell an adult so a vet can check them
column4: rabbit teeth keep growing and can stop it eating if they are not worn down

column2: a rabbit has stopped eating or doing droppings
column3: tell an adult at once
column4: this can be a sign of a gut problem that is an emergency for rabbits

column2: guinea pigs squeak loudly when you open the fridge
column3: give them a little fresh vegetable such as pepper or leafy greens
column4: guinea pigs need vitamin C every day because their bodies cannot make it

column2: keeping a guinea pig on its own
column3: keep at least two together
column4: guinea pigs are herd animals and get lonely without a friend

column2: a hamster is asleep in the daytime
column3: do not wake it; play with it in the evening
column4: hamsters are active at night and may bite if woken

column2: putting two adult Syrian hamsters in one cage
column3: keep Syrian hamsters alone
column4: adult Syrian hamsters fight, sometimes badly

column2: a hamster running in a small wheel with a bent back
column3: use a wheel big enough for its back to stay straight
column4: a small wheel can hurt a hamster's spine

column2: holding a hamster
column3: scoop it up in two cupped hands and sit close to the floor
column4: hamsters wriggle, and a fall even from a short height can kill them

column2: a hamster ball
column3: use it only for short times with an adult, never near stairs, or skip it
column4: the hamster cannot escape, can get too hot and may crash into things

column2: a hamster's cheeks are full
column3: it is carrying food to its store; leave it alone
column4: hamsters carry food in cheek pouches to hide it in their nest

column2: cleaning the hamster cage
column3: spot clean dirty bedding often and leave some old bedding so it smells like home
column4: a cage that smells completely new can stress a hamster

column2: a goldfish in a small round bowl
column3: goldfish need a large tank with a filter
column4: goldfish grow big and make a lot of waste; small bowls make them ill

column2: feeding fish a lot because they look hungry
column3: feed only a little, what they eat in a couple of minutes
column4: uneaten food rots and poisons the water

column2: tapping on the aquarium glass
column3: do not tap the glass
column4: the noise is loud and frightening for fish

column2: adding tap water to a fish tank
column3: use water treated with a dechlorinator and at the right temperature
column4: chlorine in tap water can kill fish

column2: a fish floating at the top or gasping
column3: tell an adult and check the water
column4: it may be ill or the water may be dirty or short of oxygen

column2: letting a pet fish go in a pond or river
column3: never release pet fish into the wild
column4: they can spread disease and harm native wildlife

column2: believing goldfish have a three-second memory
column3: treat fish as animals that can learn
column4: goldfish can remember things for months and learn feeding times

column2: winning a goldfish at a fair
column3: only bring it home if you are ready with a proper tank
column4: fair fish often fall ill from the trip and a bag or bowl

column2: washing hands after cleaning the fish tank
column3: wash your hands with soap
column4: tank water can carry germs such as salmonella

column2: a budgie kept alone in a small cage
column3: budgies need a friend, a big cage and time to fly in a safe room
column4: they are flock birds and get bored and lonely

column2: letting a pet bird fly in the house
column3: close windows and doors, cover mirrors and turn off fans first
column4: birds fly into glass and fans and can escape through gaps

column2: cooking with non-stick pans near a pet bird
column3: keep birds out of the kitchen
column4: fumes from overheated non-stick pans can kill birds quickly

column2: giving a parrot avocado or chocolate
column3: never feed these to birds
column4: both are poisonous to pet birds

column2: covering the bird cage at night
column3: it is fine to cover part of the cage so the bird can sleep in the dark and quiet
column4: birds need about ten to twelve hours of sleep

column2: holding a pet lizard or tortoise
column3: wash your hands with soap after every touch
column4: reptiles often carry salmonella germs even when they look healthy

column2: a pet bearded dragon or snake needs warmth
column3: keep its lamp and heat mat on as set up by an adult
column4: reptiles cannot make their own body heat and get ill if cold

column2: a pet tortoise in winter
column3: follow a vet's advice about hibernation
column4: hibernating in the wrong way can make a tortoise very ill

column2: picking up a lizard by its tail
column3: never hold a lizard by its tail
column4: many lizards can drop their tail to escape, which is stressful for them

column2: asking for a pet for your birthday
column3: talk about who will feed, clean and walk it every day for its whole life
column4: a pet lives for years and needs care every single day

column2: choosing a pet
column3: look for a rescue centre or a good breeder, and learn about the animal first
column4: pets from bad sellers are often ill, and every animal needs different care

column2: feeding the pet before your own breakfast
column3: make it a habit to check food and water every morning
column4: pets depend on you and cannot get food themselves

column2: the water bowl is empty or dirty
column3: wash it and fill it with fresh water
column4: animals need clean water all the time, especially in hot weather

column2: giving pets leftovers from your plate
column3: feed your pet its own food
column4: onions, garlic, chocolate, grapes, salt and xylitol sweetener can make pets very ill

column2: washing hands after stroking a pet
column3: wash your hands before eating and after touching pets, their bowls or their cages
column4: animals can carry germs that make people ill

column2: letting a pet lick your face
column3: do not let pets lick your mouth or face
column4: animals' mouths carry germs

column2: going on holiday
column3: arrange for a trusted person or pet sitter to look after your pet
column4: pets cannot be left alone for days

column2: a pet getting fat
column3: give fewer treats and more play
column4: overweight pets get ill and live shorter lives

column2: the vet visit
column3: keep the pet calm in its carrier and hold it as the vet tells you
column4: vets check health, give vaccines and find problems early

column2: a pet gets lost
column3: tell an adult, search nearby, call local vets and shelters and put up posters
column4: a microchip and a name tag help a lost pet come home

column2: a new pet comes home
column3: give it a quiet place and a few days to settle before lots of handling
column4: moving house is scary for animals

column2: a new baby or another pet joins the family
column3: introduce slowly and always with an adult watching
column4: animals can feel jealous or scared of newcomers

column2: a friend's pet at their house
column3: ask your friend or their parent before you touch or feed it
column4: the owner knows how the animal behaves

column2: giving a pet as a surprise present
column3: never give an animal as a surprise gift
column4: the person may not be able to care for it, and many such pets are given up

column2: deciding to stop looking after a pet you are tired of
column3: keep caring for it, and if the family really cannot, find it a new home through a shelter
column4: pets are a responsibility, and abandoning them is cruel and against the law

column2: ticks on your pet after a walk in long grass
column3: tell an adult, who will remove the tick with a tick tool
column4: ticks can spread diseases to animals and people

column2: your pet scratching all the time
column3: tell an adult and check for fleas
column4: fleas make pets itchy and can bite people too

column2: worming and flea treatment
column3: let an adult give the treatment the vet suggests
column4: it keeps pets and the family free of parasites

column2: teasing a pet with a toy and never letting it win
column3: let the pet catch the toy sometimes
column4: play that ends in frustration makes animals stressed or snappy

column2: dressing a pet up in clothes
column3: only if the animal is calm and the clothes do not restrict it, and stop if it struggles
column4: most animals do not like clothes and some get very stressed

column2: a pet left in the sun in its cage
column3: move cages and hutches into shade
column4: small animals can overheat and die quickly

column2: a pet in a hutch on a freezing night
column3: tell an adult to move it to a sheltered place and add bedding
column4: small animals can get dangerously cold

column2: putting a collar on a pet
column3: you should fit two fingers under the collar
column4: too tight hurts, too loose slips off

column2: a pet hides more than usual
column3: tell an adult
column4: hiding can mean an animal is ill, in pain or frightened

column2: a dog with its tail tucked between its legs
column3: give it space and speak softly
column4: a tucked tail means the dog is scared

column2: a cat with puffed up fur and an arched back
column3: move away and leave it alone
column4: it is very frightened and ready to defend itself

column2: a dog play-bows with its front legs down and bottom up
column3: you may play gently
column4: this bow is an invitation to play

column2: a pet that used to be friendly suddenly snaps
column3: stop touching it and tell an adult
column4: sudden grumpiness is often a sign of pain

column2: a horse with ears pinned flat back
column3: move away from it
column4: flat ears warn that the horse is angry and may bite or kick

column2: a dog panting a lot on a cool day
column3: tell an adult
column4: heavy panting without exercise or heat can mean pain, fear or illness

column2: a bird fluffed up and sleepy in the daytime
column3: tell an adult
column4: a bird that sits fluffed up may be sick

column2: a pet follows you everywhere when you come home
column3: greet it calmly and give it some attention
column4: pets bond with their families and miss them when alone

column2: a pet that is bored
column3: give it toys, play, walks and new things to sniff
column4: bored animals can become unhappy and destructive

column2: your pet dies
column3: it is okay to cry and feel sad, and to talk about it with your family
column4: grief is the natural feeling when we lose someone we love

column2: wanting to say goodbye to a pet that died
column3: draw a picture, write a letter, plant a flower or have a small ceremony
column4: remembering a pet helps the sadness slowly get smaller

column2: an old pet is very ill and the vet talks about putting it to sleep
column3: ask your parents questions and say goodbye if you can
column4: vets can end an animal's suffering painlessly when it cannot get better

column2: feeling it was your fault that the pet died
column3: talk to an adult about it
column4: children often blame themselves wrongly; most pets die of old age or illness

column2: a friend's pet has died
column3: say you are sorry and listen if they want to talk
column4: kind words help a friend who is sad

column2: getting a new pet straight after one died
column3: wait until the family is ready
column4: a new pet does not replace the old one, and each animal deserves a fresh start

column2: a pet goes missing for a long time
column3: keep checking shelters and posters and talk about how you feel
column4: not knowing is hard, and many lost pets are found again

column2: burying a pet in the garden
column3: ask an adult and dig deep enough, or ask the vet about other choices
column4: some places have rules, and a shallow grave can be dug up by animals

column2: sneezing and itchy eyes when stroking a cat
column3: tell an adult; you may be allergic
column4: many people react to proteins in pet skin flakes and saliva

column2: wheezing near animals
column3: tell an adult straight away and use your inhaler if you have one
column4: animal allergies can trigger asthma

column2: visiting a friend with a pet when you are allergic
column3: tell your friend's parent before you come
column4: they may keep the pet in another room and you can bring your medicine

column2: believing some dog breeds cause no allergies at all
column3: know that no dog is completely allergy-free
column4: some breeds shed less, but all dogs make the proteins people react to

column2: a classmate is allergic to the class pet
column3: wash your hands after touching the pet and do not bring fur near them
column4: even fur on clothes can make them ill

column2: a bee sting when someone is allergic
column3: call the emergency number at once and help them use their adrenaline pen if they have one
column4: some people have a dangerous allergic reaction called anaphylaxis

column2: walking behind a horse
column3: walk around a horse well away from its back legs, or close with a hand on it and talking
column4: a startled horse can kick backwards very hard

column2: feeding a horse a carrot or apple
column3: ask the owner, then hold your hand flat with the food on the palm
column4: fingers can be mistaken for food and bitten

column2: approaching a horse
column3: come from the side towards its shoulder, speaking softly
column4: horses cannot see directly in front of their nose or behind them

column2: riding a horse or pony
column3: always wear a riding helmet and proper boots
column4: falls from horses can cause serious head injuries

column2: horses in a field by a footpath
column3: do not feed them or climb into the field without the owner
column4: wrong food can make horses very ill, and a group of horses can be dangerous

column2: passing a horse and rider on a bike or on foot
column3: slow down, give lots of room and say hello so the horse knows you are human
column4: sudden noises and movement can scare horses

column2: believing horses sleep only standing up
column3: horses can doze standing up but lie down for deep sleep
column4: their legs lock so they can rest standing

column2: visiting a farm and touching the animals
column3: wash your hands with soap and water after touching animals, not just with gel
column4: farm animals can carry germs like E. coli that make children very ill

column2: eating a snack at the petting farm
column3: eat only after washing hands, in the picnic area
column4: germs from animals can get into your mouth from your hands

column2: cows in a field you are walking through
column3: walk calmly around them and close every gate behind you
column4: cows protecting calves can charge, and open gates let animals escape

column2: cows chase you when you have a dog
column3: let go of the dog's lead and get to safety
column4: the cows chase the dog, and the dog can outrun them

column2: a bull in a field
column3: do not enter the field
column4: bulls can be very dangerous

column2: feeding farm animals bread or garden food over a fence
column3: only feed what the farmer gives you
column4: the wrong food can make animals very ill

column2: a sheep on its back
column3: tell the farmer or an adult
column4: a sheep stuck on its back cannot get up and can die

column2: holding a chick at the farm
column3: hold it gently with cupped hands, sitting down
column4: chicks are fragile, and a fall can hurt them

column2: pigs are dirty
column3: know that pigs are clean and clever and roll in mud to cool down
column4: pigs cannot sweat, so mud protects them from heat and sunburn

column2: where milk and eggs come from
column3: cows give milk after having calves; hens lay eggs whether or not there is a rooster
column4: knowing this helps us respect farm animals and farmers

column2: backyard chickens
column3: collect eggs each day, keep the run clean, shut them in at night and wash hands after
column4: foxes and other predators attack at night, and chickens can carry salmonella

column2: a goat nibbles your clothes
column3: step away and keep loose things out of its reach
column4: goats explore with their mouths and chew almost anything

column2: a rooster chases you
column3: walk away calmly and tell the owner
column4: some roosters protect their hens by attacking

column2: a bee lands on you
column3: stay calm and still and let it fly away, or gently blow it off
column4: bees usually sting only if squashed or scared

column2: being stung by a bee
column3: ask an adult to scrape the sting out with a fingernail or card and put something cold on it
column4: the sting keeps pumping venom while it is in the skin

column2: being stung by a wasp
column3: wash the area, put something cold on it and tell an adult
column4: wasp stings hurt, and an adult can watch for an allergic reaction

column2: a wasp nest in the garden or a shed
column3: stay away and tell an adult; do not poke or throw things at it
column4: wasps defend their nest in large numbers

column2: drinking from a can outdoors in summer
column3: use a cup or straw and look before you drink
column4: a wasp may crawl inside and sting your mouth

column2: swatting at bees and wasps
column3: move away slowly
column4: flapping makes them more likely to sting

column2: bees on flowers in the garden
column3: leave them to work and plant flowers bees like
column4: bees pollinate flowers and many of our crops

column2: catching butterflies
column3: watch them instead, or catch them gently in a net and let them go at once
column4: their wings are fragile, and the tiny scales rub off when touched

column2: keeping a bug in a jar
column3: keep it only a short time, with air, leaves and damp, then release it where you found it
column4: insects die quickly in jars

column2: ants marching into the kitchen
column3: clean up crumbs and sticky spills and tell an adult
column4: ants come for food

column2: stepping on ants or bugs for fun
column3: leave them alone
column4: every small creature has a job in nature, and hurting them for fun is unkind

column2: mosquito bites
column3: use insect repellent made for children and cover up at dusk; do not scratch
column4: scratching can infect bites, and in some places mosquitoes spread disease

column2: ticks after a walk in long grass or woods
column3: check your body, especially hair, behind ears and knees, and tell an adult if you find one
column4: a tick should be removed whole with a tool by an adult; some ticks spread Lyme disease

column2: head lice
column3: tell an adult, do not share hats and combs, and comb with a nit comb
column4: lice spread by head-to-head contact and are common, not a sign of being dirty

column2: a ladybird on your hand
column3: let it walk and fly away
column4: ladybirds eat greenfly and help gardens

column2: a caterpillar with hairs
column3: do not touch hairy caterpillars
column4: the hairs of some caterpillars, like the oak processionary, cause rashes

column2: fireflies on a summer evening
column3: watch them but do not keep them in a jar
column4: they glow to find each other and die in jars

column2: fire ants in the southern USA or Australia
column3: keep away from mounds of soil and tell an adult if bitten many times
column4: fire ant stings burn and can cause allergic reactions

column2: a worm on the path after rain
column3: gently move it to soil or grass
column4: worms come up when the ground is wet and can dry out on paths; they keep soil healthy

column2: believing a worm cut in half becomes two worms
column3: know this is a myth and do not cut worms
column4: usually only one part survives, if any

column2: a spider in the bath
column3: catch it under a cup with a card and put it outside
column4: most house spiders are harmless and catch flies

column2: a spider's web in the garden
column3: look but do not break it
column4: spiders spend hours making webs to catch food

column2: dangerous spiders in Australia, such as the redback and funnel-web
column3: do not touch spiders; check shoes and gloves; if bitten, tell an adult and call 000
column4: a few Australian spiders have strong venom that needs hospital care

column2: black widow or brown recluse in North America
column3: do not put hands into woodpiles or dark corners; if bitten, tell an adult and get medical help
column4: these spiders can cause serious bites

column2: believing we swallow spiders in our sleep
column3: know this is a myth
column4: spiders avoid sleeping people, who vibrate and breathe

column2: being scared of spiders
column3: it is okay to feel scared; move away and ask an adult
column4: most spiders in Britain and Ireland cannot bite through human skin

column2: believing spiders are insects
column3: know spiders have eight legs and are arachnids
column4: insects have six legs

column2: seeing a snake on a walk
column3: stand still, then back away slowly and give it lots of space
column4: snakes usually bite only if trapped, stepped on or touched

column2: a snake in the garden or house in Australia
column3: keep away, keep pets inside and call an adult or a snake catcher
column4: many Australian snakes are venomous

column2: being bitten by a snake in Australia
column3: stay still, call 000, and an adult applies a pressure bandage
column4: staying still slows the venom from spreading

column2: a rattlesnake rattles in the USA
column3: back away slowly
column4: the rattle is a warning; give it space

column2: being bitten by any snake
column3: call the emergency number, stay calm and still, and do not suck the bite or cut it
column4: sucking and cutting do not work and cause harm

column2: the adder, the only venomous snake in Britain
column3: leave it alone; if bitten, keep still and get medical help
column4: adder bites are rare and treatable but need hospital checks

column2: believing there are snakes in Ireland or New Zealand
column3: know there are no wild land snakes in Ireland or New Zealand
column4: they never reached these islands; snakes in New Zealand must be reported

column2: walking in long grass in snake country
column3: wear boots and long trousers and stay on paths
column4: most bites happen to feet and legs

column2: believing snakes are slimy
column3: know a snake's skin is dry and smooth
column4: it looks shiny because of its scales

column2: a baby bird on the ground
column3: leave it unless it is in danger; its parents are usually nearby
column4: young birds often leave the nest before they can fly and are fed on the ground

column2: a baby bird with no feathers on the ground
column3: tell an adult, who may put it back in the nest or call a wildlife rescue
column4: naked chicks cannot survive outside the nest

column2: believing a mother bird will reject a chick that people touched
column3: know this is a myth, but still touch wild animals only when needed
column4: most birds have a weak sense of smell

column2: finding an injured wild animal
column3: do not pick it up; tell an adult, who can call a wildlife rescue
column4: injured animals may bite and need expert care

column2: feeding ducks bread
column3: feed them oats, peas or duck food in small amounts
column4: bread fills ducks up without nourishing them and dirties the water

column2: a fox in the garden
column3: watch from a window and do not feed or try to touch it
column4: foxes are wild and can carry mange and diseases

column2: a hedgehog in the garden in the UK or Ireland
column3: leave a shallow dish of water or meaty cat food, never milk or bread
column4: milk makes hedgehogs ill

column2: a hedgehog out in the daytime
column3: tell an adult, who can call a hedgehog rescue
column4: hedgehogs are night animals, so one out in daylight may be sick

column2: squirrels at the park
column3: watch them but do not hand-feed them
column4: squirrels can bite and get too used to people

column2: a bat in the house
column3: do not touch it; leave the room, shut the door and tell an adult
column4: bats can carry rabies in some places and must only be handled with gloves by experts

column2: raccoons in the bins in North America
column3: do not go near them and keep bins closed
column4: raccoons can bite and carry rabies

column2: a bear in the woods in Canada or the USA
column3: stay with adults, do not run, speak calmly and back away slowly
column4: running can make a bear chase you

column2: camping where bears live
column3: keep food in a bear box or car, never in the tent
column4: bears are attracted by food smells

column2: a skunk raises its tail in North America
column3: back away quietly
column4: skunks spray a terrible smell when they feel threatened

column2: kangaroos in Australia
column3: watch from a distance and do not feed them
column4: big kangaroos can kick and scratch badly

column2: magpies swooping in Australian spring
column3: walk quickly through, wear a hat, and do not throw things back
column4: magpies swoop to protect their nests for a few weeks in spring

column2: a koala or wombat on the road
column3: tell an adult and keep away
column4: wild animals hurt on roads should be helped by wildlife rescue

column2: seeing a kiwi or other native bird in New Zealand
column3: keep dogs on leads in kiwi areas and stay quiet
column4: many native birds are endangered and dogs can kill them

column2: alligators in Florida and the southern USA
column3: stay well away from the water's edge in alligator areas
column4: alligators can move fast and attack

column2: crocodiles in northern Australia
column3: never swim where crocodiles live and stay away from the edge
column4: crocodiles hide in water and attack suddenly

column2: a deer in the woods
column3: watch quietly from a distance
column4: deer are easily frightened, and stags can be dangerous in autumn

column2: a fawn or young hare alone in a field
column3: leave it; the mother comes back to feed it
column4: mothers leave young alone to keep them hidden

column2: a mouse or rat in the house
column3: tell an adult and do not touch it or its droppings
column4: rodents can carry diseases

column2: a wild animal acting oddly tame or strange
column3: keep away and tell an adult
column4: it may be sick, sometimes with rabies

column2: birds in the garden in winter
column3: put out seeds and fresh water
column4: food is hard to find in cold weather

column2: a bird hits the window
column3: tell an adult; put the stunned bird in a box in a quiet dark place
column4: most stunned birds recover after a rest

column2: frogspawn in a pond
column3: look but leave it in the pond
column4: frogs are protected, and tadpoles need their pond to grow

column2: turning over logs and stones to look for creatures
column3: put them back the way you found them
column4: small animals live under them

column2: collecting shells with animals inside
column3: leave living creatures where they are
column4: they die when taken from their home

column2: feeding wild animals at a campsite or park
column3: never feed wild animals
column4: it makes them sick, dependent and sometimes dangerous

column2: a bird's nest in a hedge in spring
column3: watch quietly from far away
column4: scaring the parents can make them leave their eggs

column2: seagulls snatching your food at the beach
column3: eat in a sheltered spot and do not feed them
column4: feeding teaches gulls to grab food

column2: rock pooling
column3: look gently, put creatures back where you found them, and watch the tide
column4: sea creatures can die out of water, and the tide can cut you off

column2: a jellyfish on the beach
column3: do not touch it, even if it looks dead
column4: dead jellyfish can still sting

column2: a seal on the beach
column3: stay well back, at least 10 metres, keep dogs on a lead and tell an adult if it looks hurt
column4: seals rest on land and can bite

column2: believing bats are blind
column3: know bats can see, and many also use echoes to find their way
column4: this is called echolocation

column2: believing owls can turn their heads all the way round
column3: know they can turn about three quarters of the way
column4: they cannot move their eyes, so they turn their heads

column2: visiting the zoo
column3: follow signs, stay behind barriers and do not climb fences
column4: zoo animals are wild and can be dangerous

column2: feeding zoo animals
column3: only feed animals when a keeper says so
column4: the wrong food can make them very ill

column2: banging on glass or shouting at zoo animals
column3: watch quietly
column4: noise stresses the animals

column2: throwing things into enclosures
column3: never throw anything in
column4: animals may eat it and get hurt

column2: an animal is hiding at the zoo
column3: be patient and come back later
column4: animals need places to rest out of sight

column2: getting lost at the zoo
column3: go to a keeper or the information desk and wait
column4: staff can help find your family

column2: why zoos keep animals
column3: good zoos protect endangered animals and teach people about them
column4: some species survive today only thanks to zoo breeding

column2: flash photos of animals
column3: turn off the flash
column4: bright flashes can frighten animals, especially in dark houses

column2: the touch pool at an aquarium
column3: touch with two fingers gently, as the staff show
column4: sea creatures are delicate and can be hurt by rough handling

column2: wanting a pet from a pet shop
column3: ask questions about how big it grows and how long it lives
column4: many animals grow much bigger and live longer than people think

column2: thinking sharks want to eat people
column3: know sharks rarely attack people
column4: we are not their normal food

column2: seeing someone hurt an animal
column3: tell a trusted adult
column4: animal cruelty is wrong and can be reported to an animal welfare organisation

column2: a cat or dog seems abandoned
column3: tell an adult, who can call the local animal shelter
column4: shelters can find the owner or a new home

column2: helping at an animal shelter
column3: ask if your family can donate food, blankets or toys
column4: shelters need help caring for animals

column2: teasing an animal in a cage or behind a fence
column3: never tease animals
column4: it causes fear and stress and can make them aggressive

column2: using a magnifying glass on bugs in the sun
column3: never do that
column4: it burns them

column2: leaving litter outside
column3: throw it away properly
column4: animals get trapped in plastic or eat it

column2: fishing line and hooks left by water
column3: tell an adult or put them in a bin
column4: birds and animals get tangled

column2: balloons released into the sky
column3: do not release balloons
column4: they fall and animals eat them or get tangled

column2: cutting the rings of a drink pack
column3: cut plastic rings before throwing them away
column4: animals can get trapped in them

column2: chasing pigeons or ducks
column3: watch them calmly
column4: chasing frightens and tires them

column2: leaving a bucket of water in the garden
column3: cover it or put a stick in for animals to climb out
column4: small animals can fall in and drown

column2: bonfire piles before lighting
column3: check them for hedgehogs before lighting
column4: hedgehogs like to hide in piles of sticks

column2: garden netting
column3: keep it tight or remove it
column4: loose netting traps birds and hedgehogs

column2: slug pellets and rat poison in the shed
column3: never touch them and keep pets away
column4: poisons can kill pets and wildlife

column2: being gentle with small animals
column3: always move slowly and speak softly
column4: animals feel safe with calm people
